editorNote: Adventure, music and color give the home computer new work to do.
morningLine: Crichton maps a different kind of adventure; the Commodore learns new tunes.

lead.headline: Michael Crichton trades the movie screen for the adventure game
lead.dek: In a February interview, the author behind Amazon explains why story should guide the player.
body: Michael Crichton wants the computer adventure to tell a story, not merely conceal a solution. Interviewed by Betsy Staples in February’s Creative Computing, the novelist and filmmaker describes Amazon, his Trillium Software adventure made with programmer Stephen Warady, as a sequence of dramatic episodes.

A river crossing, a volcano climb and a journey to a Lost City form the expedition. Crichton compares the arrangement to beads on a string: individual challenges serve the trip. “My interest is not in creating a puzzle space; my interest is in trying to tell a story in a new way,” he says.

The author did more than supply a name for the package. He supplied a text flowchart, location map and color graphics frames, along with BASIC portions subsequently translated into machine language. His contributions included main-title graphics, in-game computer modules and sound effects.

Crichton sees room for an eventual family entertainment form between films and computer games, though he cautions that it will not arrive this year. His own collection ranges from an IBM PC/AT to a Commodore 64; for travel, he favors the TRS-80 Model 100. Amazon is a current adventure under discussion this month, not a newly announced release this week.

stories.headline: A $239 color printer meets the real-paper test
body: Color printing reaches the Commodore desk at a quoted $239 with interface. Charles Brannon’s February Gazette review examines the Okimate-10, whose nine-wire thermal-transfer element melts waxlike ribbon ink onto paper. The process is quieter than impact printing.

The paper matters as much as the mechanism. Brannon reports unacceptable results on ordinary fanfold, photocopy and bond paper, while acetate gives clear, sharp images. The supplied glossy paper is acceptable but light. A bargain printer still asks the buyer to choose supplies carefully.

The $169.95 base unit requires its proprietary interface; a generic printer interface will not substitute. Black ribbons are quoted at $5.95 and rated by Okidata for roughly 75 average text pages. They cannot be reused. These are February review prices and manufacturer claims, not a nationwide store-price survey.

stories.headline: The Commodore 64 becomes a music room for non-musicians
body: The Commodore 64’s music circuit is finding new companions. February’s Gazette describes Sight & Sound’s work with jazz guitarist Ryo Kawasaki on software for its keyboard accessory. The series runs from $29.95 to $49.95.

Kawasaki Synthesizer makes the machine a programmable synthesizer and sound processor. Kawasaki Rhythm Rocker joins electronic rhythms, sound effects and high-resolution graphics. Music Processor handles composing, editing, recording and playback; 3001: A Sound Odyssey teaches, while Music Video Kit turns toward pictures.

Waveform’s Colortone Keyboard takes another approach: a $79.95 touch-sensitive membrane with 25 piano-like keys, a harp strip and 14 function keys. Its supplied software offers eight instrument sounds and 12 songs. These are products described in the February feature, not new weekly shipping announcements.

stories.headline: IBM announces its 3090 mainframe family
body: IBM announced the 3090 Models 200 and 400 on February 12. The new large-system family brings a two-central-processor Model 200 and a four-processor Model 400 configuration formed from two 200 systems.

The announcement sits far from the home-computer shelf, but marks the week’s clearest dated computing development. The New York Times followed on February 13 with “Sierra Adds Power to I.B.M.” No price is established here. The later 3090 vector facility is not part of this February announcement.

posts.text: Editorial paraphrase, not an authentic BBS post: stores and user groups can point callers toward boards, and boards advertise other boards.

posts.topic: Busy signals are a sign of success
posts.text: Editorial paraphrase: growing membership makes single-line boards harder to reach and can prompt membership fees to support the sysop.

posts.platform: CompuServe / The Source / Dow Jones / Delphi
posts.text: Editorial paraphrase: national-service connect time generally starts around $6 an hour or more; time, speed and telephone distance matter. No invented user handles or historical message transcripts.

curiosity.headline: Break-dancing comes home to the Commodore
curiosity.summary: Creative Software sells a dancing program instead of another space battle.
curiosity.detail: The February Gazette ad for Break Street names moonwalk, backspin, windmill and tut, offers slow motion, and lets players string moves together and record them for replay. This is evidence of an advertised February product, not a release that week.

periodAd.headline: Bank Street Writer — $49.95
periodAd.summary: Broderbund’s C64 advertisement offers prompts, menus, search and replace, page formatting, documentation and a backup disk at $49.95 suggested retail.

market.headline: The cost of going online
market.summary: February Gazette distinguishes mostly free local bulletin boards from metered commercial services, generally $6 or more per connected hour depending on time and speed. Long-distance telephone tolls remain a separate expense; even a free board can cost money to call.
